Moreover, supply chain vulnerabilities are pronounced, with the United States importing 99% of the uranium concentrate used in existing nuclear generators in 2023 (EIA 2025a). In 2023, leading foreign sources included (as percentages of total deliveries) Canada (27%), Australia (22%), Kazakhstan (22%), Russia (12%), and Uzbekistan (10%). The United States also imports enriched uranium, as domestic enrichment capacity provided for only 30% of uranium fuel needs in 2023, with more than 20% of these imports being sourced from Russia as of the same year (Roy and Dareen 2024). Although the United States adopted a ban on uranium products from Russia in 2024, companies can apply for a waiver through 2027 (EIA 2025a). U.S. production of uranium concentrate increased in 2024, at five facilities in Texas and Wyoming, and total employment in the U.S. uranium production industry increased 49% from 2023 to 2024 (EIA 2025b). A U.S. White House executive order in March 2025 announced the prioritization of domestic critical mineral access, production, and processing, including uranium (The White House 2025), which could also encourage more domestic production. Further, many SMR designs would use “high-assay low-enriched uranium,” which is not yet widely produced (Office of Nuclear Energy 2024). The United States and allies would need to substantially increase uranium concentrate production and enrichment capacity to avoid supply chain vulnerabilities for the expanded demand that widespread SMR deployment would introduce. Competition to lead the industry could exacerbate supply chain risks, given that China and Russia lead in SMR deployment. Supply chain vulnerabilities will be especially acute if China accelerates commercialization and comes to dominate the supply chain for SMRs as it has for lithium-ion batteries and solar PV. Although radioactive waste generation by SMRs has not been thoroughly researched, one study reported that SMRs produce a greater volume of radioactive waste than traditional larger-scale reactors, by a factor of 2 to 30, creating a need for waste handling and disposal (Shwartz 2022). In addition, the potential exportation of SMR technologies presents a nuclear proliferation risk. Russia’s two 35-MW(e) floating SMRs have been operational since 2020, and China’s 200- MW(e) capacity demonstration project has been operational since 2023. Argentina, Canada, South Korea, and the United Kingdom are planning or developing SMRs. Denmark, South Korea, Russia, and China are developing floating SMR designs. U.S.-based Holtec International is developing a 300-MW SMR (IAEA 2024); it is working with the state of Utah to develop a training facility for skilled workers in Utah, and it is planning to produce and deploy these reactors for deployment in Utah and other western states (Kaufman 2025).
